documents.unit: Division of Information Resources & Technology and Office of the Provost
documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy (University Policies)
documents.summary: An information-security policy for the whole university. It bans putting confidential data into public AI tools, limits university business to approved platforms, and covers AI recording, procurement, copyright and research. On coursework it only says to follow the Academic Integrity Policy.
documents.stance_why: The only coursework sentence is 'AI requirements related to coursework must comply with the Academic Integrity Policy', so the document sets no stance on student AI use and hands the question to other policies. Its own rules (e.g. 'must not enter ... confidential ... data into publicly-available AI tools') concern data security, not coursework, so delegates fits best.

units.why: States the policy's purpose, 'secure use of AI and Large Language Models', so it is a framework statement for the whole institution (P56), informational rather than a rule.
units.anchor: establish requirements for the secure use of AI and Large Language Models (LLM)

units.why: Scope sentence: 'applies to all members of the Rowan Community'. It sets who the framework binds, which fits P56 (purpose, scope, principles) rather than a definition type.
units.anchor: applies to all members of the Rowan Community

units.why: Names who implements the policy ('Vice Presidents and Deans shall implement'), which is ownership and enforcement assignment (P80).
units.anchor: The Vice Presidents and Deans shall implement this policy.

units.why: A rule that AI use 'must adhere to all Rowan University policies' ties AI to existing policy, which is P77 (comply with existing law and policy).
units.anchor: The use of AI tools must adhere to all Rowan University policies

units.why: Requires everyone to follow legal, ethical and university standards on 'data use, privacy, consent, ownership, and academic integrity', i.e. compliance with existing law and policy (P77).
units.anchor: must adhere to human resource and legal requirements, as well as ethical standards

units.why: Warns employees that 'AI generated transcripts of meetings may create records subject to OPRA', a legal-compliance duty (P77); P86 (consent to recording) fits less because it concerns records law, not permission to record.
units.anchor: AI generated transcripts of meetings may create records subject to OPRA
units.fit_note: Also touches AI meeting transcription, but the point is public-records law.

units.why: Flat ban ('must not enter ... confidential ... data into publicly-available AI tools') on putting sensitive data into AI, which is data protection (P50).
units.anchor: must not enter Rowan internal, confidential, proprietary or regulated data

units.why: Requires university business, 'including academic', to run only in 'officially approved AI/LLM platforms', so use the approved tools (P92) rather than a general data-protection type.
units.anchor: must only be processed in officially approved AI/LLM platforms

units.why: Stated as an absolute: 'No University business information may be processed on any unapproved platform', the negative form of the approved-tools rule (P92).
units.anchor: No University business information may be processed on any unapproved platform.

units.why: Purchases of AI services 'must be procured through' IRT and Procurement, an institutional review and approval gate for AI tools (P65).
units.anchor: must be procured through the standard processes of the Division of Information Resources

units.why: Limits AI recording of meetings to IRT-authorized platforms: 'may only be recorded by AI platforms that are authorized', which is a recording rule (P86).
units.anchor: may only be recorded by AI platforms that are authorized, secured and managed by IRT
units.fit_note: Condition is IRT authorization, not consent of participants.

units.why: Says HR meeting AI transcriptions 'should not be used' without prior HR permission and safeguards: permission before AI transcription (P86).
units.anchor: AI transcriptions of confidential Human Resources meetings

units.why: The only coursework sentence: it sets no AI stance but sends coursework to the 'Academic Integrity Policy', i.e. compliance with existing policy (P77); it does not set a rule of its own, so P04 does not fit.
units.anchor: AI requirements related to coursework must comply with the

units.why: Names offices that field questions on AI use ('Office of Ethics, Academic Integrity or Research'), which designates who interprets the policy (P80).
units.anchor: should be directed to the Rowan University Office of Ethics, Academic Integrity or Research

units.why: 'May not infringe on copyright laws' limits AI use by copyright and university copyright policy (P52).
units.anchor: The use of AI may not infringe on copyright laws

units.why: Defers research AI use to 'applicable policies and governing Research', which is the research-and-scholarship type (P62).
units.anchor: AI use in Research, including the development of AI and other machine learning

units.why: States penalties for violating the policy ('discipline up to and including dismissal'). Closest is concrete penalties (P37), though it covers employee discipline, not student misuse.
units.anchor: subject to discipline up to and including dismissal from the University
units.fit_note: Penalties apply to any violator of this security policy, mostly employees, not students' academic misconduct.

units.why: Names who grants exceptions ('approved by the Information Security Office and Office of the Provost'), the exception process in P80.
units.anchor: Any exceptions to this policy must be approved by the Information Security Office

documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence & Teaching
tiers: Generic statement deferring to instructor guidelines (Option 4)
documents.summary: Faculty Center page that says Rowan has no universal GenAI policy, recommends a syllabus statement and offers four sample statements from no AI to some AI. It also gives advice on detectors, citations and follow-up with students, plus many resource links.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'The University does not have a universal generative AI policy' and offers sample statements instead, with Option 4 saying 'you must follow all instructor guidelines'. Because it provides templates and leaves the choice to instructors, the stance is delegates with the tiers listed.

units.why: A University Senate task force recommendation that faculty 'include a clear and specific statement in their syllabi and Canvas', i.e. an AI statement in every syllabus (P09); it is 'should', not 'must'.
units.anchor: Faculty should include a clear and specific statement in their syllabi and Canvas

units.why: Says no single university rule exists and leaves it to instructors ('Instructors may select one of the following statements'), which is letting the instructor set the rule (P04).
units.anchor: The University does not have a universal generative AI policy.

units.why: Offers a menu of four sample syllabus statements from 'No generative AI' to 'Some generative AI', which are templates at different levels of use (P05).
units.anchor: Instructors may select one of the following statements if appropriate to their classroom.

units.why: Option 1 sample text bans 'any use of generative artificial intelligence' in the course, a default ban (P01).
units.anchor: any use of generative artificial intelligence such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, Claude, Copilot, Gemini
units.policy: Sample statement (Option 1): any use of generative AI in the course is a violation of academic integrity.

units.why: Lists sanctions in advance ('fail the assignment, fail the course, or face other sanctions') in the Option 1 text: concrete penalties (P37).
units.anchor: students committing any act of academic dishonesty may fail the assignment, fail the course

units.why: A procedural duty ('must be reported to the Provost's Office') once a penalty is given, the formal integrity-reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: Violations that result in a grade penalty must be reported to the Provost's Office.

units.why: Asks students to document use of 'the language or ideas of others', a general attribution rule inside the no-AI template (P24); it does not name AI, hence the fit note.
units.anchor: students should provide appropriate documentation whenever quoting, paraphrasing, summarizing
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI itself; general attribution advice in the Option 1 template.

units.why: Option 2 grounds the ban in assignments that 'help you develop key skills' and 'assess whether you have mastered', which explains that AI shortcuts skill-building practice (P41).
units.anchor: to help you develop key skills and to assess whether you have mastered

units.why: Option 2 text bans generative AI on the assignments ('defeats the purpose ... academic integrity violation'), a default prohibition (P01) rather than only a rationale.
units.anchor: Using generative AI or other unauthorized tools on these assignments defeats the purpose

units.why: Option 2 tells students to ask the instructor when unsure about allowed resources ('please let me know'), which is P10.
units.anchor: what resources may be allowed on a specific assignment please let me know

units.why: Option 3 requires submitted work to be the student's own, 'not the work of an AI system': the no-AI-produced-work rule (P19).
units.anchor: should be that of the student and not the work of an AI system

units.why: Option 3 allows AI 'to support learning (e.g., in obtaining feedback or generating ideas)'. Ideas fits brainstorming (P15); feedback is not captured, so noted.
units.anchor: tool to support learning (e.g., in obtaining feedback or generating ideas)
units.fit_note: Also permits obtaining feedback, which P15 does not name.

units.why: Option 3 says AI-generated material 'should be cited like any other reference material', a disclosure-by-citation rule (P24); the comparison to other references is secondary.
units.anchor: it should be cited like any other reference material

units.why: Option 3 puts responsibility for errors on the student ('bears responsibility for any inaccuracies'). Chosen P29 (owns what is submitted) over P31 because it assigns accountability, not a duty to verify.
units.anchor: the student bears responsibility for any inaccuracies or misinformation

units.why: Option 3 asks students with questions about AI use to 'reach out to your instructor': ask before using (P10).
units.anchor: please reach out to your instructor

units.why: Option 4 (generic) makes students follow whatever the instructor decides on 'use or prohibition': responsibility to learn and follow the course's rules (P78); the instructor-decides element is P04 but P78 is the student duty stated.
units.anchor: you must follow all instructor guidelines on the use or prohibition of generative AI
units.fit_note: Also delegates the stance to the instructor.

units.why: Option 4 classes 'unauthorized use of generative AI' as possible 'cheating' under the integrity policy, which is P36.
units.anchor: The unauthorized use of generative AI on assignments may be considered cheating

units.why: Option 4 makes missing citation the violation: 'without citation is considered plagiarism' (P28, nondisclosure as the violation).
units.anchor: Submitting the output of generative AI without citation is considered plagiarism

units.why: Option 4 repeats student responsibility ('you are responsible for any inaccuracies') for submitted work: P29.
units.anchor: you are responsible for any inaccuracies or information within your submitted assignments

units.why: Option 4 invites students to ask the instructor for clarification, i.e. ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: please do not hesitate to reach out to your instructor for clarification

units.why: Option 4 concedes AI 'can be used as a tool to support learning', which states a benefit of AI without making it a rule (P87).
units.anchor: it is possible for generative AI to be used as a tool to support learning

units.why: Suggests faculty 'list the ways that generative AI could be used' on assignments, advice about stating expectations (P09), optional rather than required.
units.anchor: Faculty also might choose to list the ways that generative AI could be used
units.fit_note: Optional advice to detail permitted uses; P09 is about a required statement.

units.why: Points to a page on 'Rowan-licensed GenAI tools and guidelines', university-wide approved tools (P92); it is institution-wide, so not P17.
units.anchor: an overview of Rowan-licensed GenAI tools and guidelines for using them

units.why: Links a repository of other instructors' syllabus policies 'to help in the development of their own', faculty support for setting course policy (P63).
units.anchor: helping other instructors see the range of policies available by other educators

units.why: A heading with APA and MLA links for citing AI shows the university directs people to citation of AI use (P24), informational only.
units.anchor: How to cite the use of AI
units.fit_note: Only links to external citation guides; no Rowan rule.

units.why: Offers an AI-literacy Canvas module for students, faculty can add to courses: AI-literacy training (P70).
units.anchor: Introduction to AI Literacy for Students is a Canvas module designed specifically for Rowan students

units.why: A Rowan video on student AI use 'can be shown in class', material to explain AI rules to students: closest P70 (guides for students) though it also supports discussion (P66).
units.anchor: This Rowan-produced video (2:20) can be shown in class or linked in your Canvas
units.fit_note: Also supports explaining the rules in class (P66).

units.why: A student AI guide with 'downloadable Teacher Guides' for any discipline is curricular AI-literacy material (P70).
units.anchor: The 2026 version contains downloadable Teacher Guides (pdfs & PowerPoints) that can be adapted

units.why: Tells faculty 'we do NOT recommend relying on' AI content detectors, the do-not-rely-on-detectors type (P39).
units.anchor: we do NOT recommend relying on any of the numerous “AI Content Detector” programs

units.why: Gives the reason for distrusting detectors: 'false positives ... false accusations made against students' (P39).
units.anchor: reports of false positives from these software systems that can lead to false accusations

units.why: A standard of evidence: detector results 'will not be considered as evidence' while 'other forms of evidence may be used'. It sets what counts as evidence (P69, which lists Rowan).
units.anchor: results from these detectors will not be considered as evidence for a Rowan Report

units.why: States that AI 'may create fictitious citations', output can be wrong or hallucinated (P31); the audience is faculty, hence the fit note.
units.anchor: may not cite them correctly or may create fictitious citations
units.fit_note: Addressed to faculty checking student work rather than to students verifying output.

units.why: Says invented sources or quotations are grounds for an integrity report: a kind of evidence to weigh (P69) and fabrication as dishonesty.
units.anchor: faculty can submit Academic Integrity Violations based on invented sources and/or quotations

units.why: Procedural requirement: 'faculty must file an AIV report' to sanction, the formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: faculty must file an AIV report if they wish to sanction a student

units.why: Advises talking with the student and asking 'follow up questions to verify their understanding' before any report: P57 (talk first). P34 also fits but the focus is the conversation before escalating.
units.anchor: Schedule a time to discuss the topic of the paper with the student

units.why: Suggests building follow-up conversations 'into the course structure so students are not singled out', which is an understanding check designed into the course (P34).
units.anchor: built into the course structure so students are not singled out

units.why: Instructs a 'nonconfrontational' approach to suspected misuse, an educative response (P68); P57 fits less because it concerns the order of steps, not tone.
units.anchor: initiate the discussion in a nonconfrontational manner

units.why: Endorses a guide to build skills 'to work with, and direct powerful AI technologies', learning to use AI as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: develop the uniquely human capabilities that allow us to work with, and direct powerful AI

units.why: Links a toolkit to help educators 'initiate important conversations about responsible AI practices', faculty support resource (P63).
units.anchor: assist educators in initiating important conversations about responsible AI practices in the classroom

units.why: Describes a linked toolkit for 'Assignment Redesign' as a 'living document': faculty support resource (P63), a pointer only, not a Rowan rule.
units.anchor: a living document, regularly updated with the latest research and best practices in pedagogy.
units.fit_note: Pointer to external redesign resource; no Rowan assessment rule.

documents.title: GenAI at Rowan: For Students
documents.summary: Student page of the library GenAI guide. It lists tools Rowan approves for data protection, warns that using GenAI without the instructor's permission may be an integrity violation, and links to citation guidance and student AI guides.
documents.stance_why: It tells students that GenAI use 'without the permission of the instructor may lead to an academic integrity violation' and to 'follow the guidelines given by your instructor for a specific course'. The decision is left to each course, so delegates.

units.why: Says the listed tools are 'approved by Rowan in terms of data protection', pointing students to university-approved AI tools (P92).
units.anchor: The tools below are approved by Rowan in terms of data protection.

units.why: Students should 'follow the guidelines given by your instructor for a specific course': learn and follow each course's AI rules (P78).
units.anchor: it is important to follow the guidelines given by your instructor for a specific course

units.why: Using GenAI 'without the permission of the instructor' risks an integrity violation, which implies AI is off unless permitted, a fallback rule (P06); also P36 but the permission default is the main content.
units.anchor: without the permission of the instructor may lead to an academic integrity violation
units.fit_note: Also classifies unpermitted use as an integrity violation with sanctions.

units.why: Students must 'check the syllabus or clarify with your instructor': finding out each course's rules (P78); the asking part overlaps P10 but the syllabus-first duty is stronger.
units.anchor: check the syllabus or clarify with your instructor whether they allow
units.fit_note: Also says to ask the instructor (P10).

units.why: Warns that tools 'make up facts, quotations and citations', AI output is often wrong (P31).
units.anchor: GenAI tools may confidently state false information, make up facts, quotations and citations

units.why: Asks students to 'engage carefully and thoughtfully with the generated content', critical evaluation of output (P31).
units.anchor: be sure to engage carefully and thoughtfully with the generated content

units.why: Describes Copilot as available to students with 'commercial data protection', stating that student data is not used for training: data protection of a vetted tool (P50).
units.anchor: Student data is not used to train the underlying language models.

units.why: Warns students that 'no way to delete Gemini chats' exists: a data-retention caveat (P50).
units.anchor: there is currently no way to delete Gemini chats in Workspace accounts

units.why: Names a licensed image tool 'available for students who are enrolled in some' courses, a university-provided tool (P92).
units.anchor: available for students who are enrolled in some College of Communication & Creative Arts

units.why: Recommends a student guide with '7 principles' for learning about GenAI and appropriate use, AI-literacy material (P70).
units.anchor: provides 7 principles to help with learning about GenAI as well as appropriate use

units.why: Recommends a guide so students can 'work with, and direct powerful AI technologies', learning AI as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: develop the uniquely human capabilities that allow us to work with, and direct powerful AI

units.why: Links APA and MLA citation guidance for AI generators, pointing to how AI use is cited (P24), with no Rowan rule of its own.
units.anchor: How to cite ChatGPT
units.fit_note: Only external links; no Rowan requirement to cite.

documents.title: Generative AI Use Policy
documents.date_or_term: cites AI tools accessed June-July 2025; no explicit date
documents.summary: A departmental policy for all undergraduate and graduate ECE courses. It welcomes AI for learning, brainstorming, debugging and proofreading, but not as the source of graded work, and lists banned uses, including code over 25 percent. It sets a detailed citation format and an oral or written check when misuse is suspected.
documents.stance_why: The summary says the department 'welcomes, even encourages, responsible and educational use' of AI as long as 'the AI generated content is not submitted as graded work', with listed allowed uses, a 25 percent code cap and required citation. AI is allowed under conditions, not banned or merely tolerated, so permit.

units.why: The summary 'welcomes, even encourages, responsible and educational use' sets AI as welcome by default, P02.
units.anchor: ECE department welcomes, even encourages, responsible and educational use of Generative AI

units.why: The welcome is limited: 'so long as the AI generated content is not submitted as graded work', the rule that AI may not produce the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: so long as the AI generated content is not submitted as graded work

units.why: Students are 'responsible for describing, justifying and/or explaining their work', explain-and-defend duty (P30).
units.anchor: ultimately responsible for describing, justifying and/or explaining their work and design

units.why: Names benefits ('extremely helpful in retrieving information, solving routine problems') without a rule: P87.
units.anchor: G-AI tools can be extremely helpful in retrieving information, solving routine problems

units.why: Warns improper AI use can 'limit your ability to understand and apply important content', reason that shortcuts hurt learning (P41); the inaccuracy half is P31.
units.anchor: limit your ability to understand and apply important content
units.fit_note: Also warns of inaccurate information.

units.why: Grounds the policy in preparing students for a workforce where 'appropriate use of these tools will be all too common': career reason to learn AI (P44).
units.anchor: prepare you not just for today’s but also the future’s job market and workforce

units.why: Says the workforce needs 'human experts who can verify the accuracy of the G-AI output', justifying verification (P31).
units.anchor: human experts who can verify the accuracy of the G-AI output

units.why: Cites graduates' work in settings 'where the use of AI is strictly restricted' as a reason to learn proper use. Nearest is P94 (careers as reason), but here the aim is to learn proper use, not skills without AI.
units.anchor: work in classified, confidential, or content-controlled areas, where the use of AI is strictly restricted
units.fit_note: Career reason is about learning how and when to use AI properly, not building skills without AI.

units.why: The department policy applies 'unless explicitly stated otherwise in a course syllabus', the default when the syllabus is silent (P06).
units.anchor: Unless explicitly stated otherwise in a course syllabus, the following applies uniformly
units.fit_note: Default is the department's own permissive-with-limits policy and the syllabus may override it.

units.why: Lists as 'appropriate and acceptable' using AI to learn and understand a topic, tutoring use (P12).
units.anchor: Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.

units.why: Lists 'idea brainstorming' as acceptable: P15.
units.anchor: Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.

units.why: Permits AI literature searches; no type covers literature search directly (summaries in P14 are study aids), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content
units.policy: AI may be used for literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content.
units.uncovered_note: Permission to use AI for literature search and paper discovery.

units.why: Requires final citations to 'be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources', i.e. verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv)

units.why: Allows AI for routine code structure under a cap: the student's own code must be '75% or higher', a percentage condition (P16).
units.anchor: 75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours

units.why: Lists 'debugging your code' as acceptable AI use: P13.
units.anchor: and/or debugging your code

units.why: Condition that the student 'understand, test, and document the code entirely': P30.
units.anchor: that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly

units.why: Says students will be asked to 'explain your code and demonstrate your understanding' as proof of authorship, understanding check (P34).
units.anchor: You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding

units.why: Permits 'routine proof-reading' if 'the original sentences are yours': P91.
units.anchor: Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences

units.why: Permits AI-generated 'non-technical figures' as concept illustrations; no type covers image generation, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations
units.policy: AI may be used to generate non-technical figures as concept illustrations, subject to course-specific permission.
units.uncovered_note: Permission for AI-generated illustrations, subject to instructor permission.

units.why: Allows AI where 'the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool', AI built into assigned work (P79).
units.anchor: the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool

units.why: Tells students unsure about a use to 'reach out to your course professor': P10.
units.anchor: please reach out to your course professor

units.why: Lists uncited AI use as 'inappropriate and not allowed': disclosure with each submission (P24).
units.anchor: Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited

units.why: AI may not solve or answer graded questions: the submitted-work ban (P19). P22 covers exams only, this covers all graded work.
units.anchor: Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.

units.why: Bans AI analysis of data and conclusions in graded work, so AI cannot produce submitted analysis (P19); P89 is the opposite permission.
units.anchor: Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis
units.fit_note: Specific to data analysis and conclusions.

units.why: Separate rule for prose: no AI for essay answers except language clarification (P18).
units.anchor: Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above)

units.why: AI may not determine impact factors, ethics or professional judgment that students must articulate, keeping the student as the thinker (P32).
units.anchor: Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course

units.why: Bans AI code over 25% of a script: a percentage cap on AI-generated code (P16).
units.anchor: Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script

units.why: When base code is given, 'modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated': AI may not produce the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work

units.why: Bans uploading course materials to 'any unauthorized G-AI tool': P49.
units.anchor: Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool

units.why: No AI for 'mathematical derivations submitted' as graded work: P19.
units.anchor: Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.

units.why: No AI for 'algorithm design submitted' as graded work: P19.
units.anchor: Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.

units.why: Bans AI-generated report sections, a prose rule (P18); uploading raw data to generate a report is the given example.
units.anchor: Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report

units.why: Bans AI interpretation of simulation results in submissions: P19; the data-analysis permission (P89) is the opposite.
units.anchor: Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
units.fit_note: Specific to simulation results.

units.why: Presenting AI-generated content as yours 'is plagiarism': misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others

units.why: Rewording to hide a source 'is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty': P36.
units.anchor: Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source

units.why: Violations 'will be reported to the Provost's Office': reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy

units.why: States lecture notes are the instructor's 'intellectual property' and copyrighted, the IP basis (P52).
units.anchor: Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor.

units.why: Uploading course content to GenAI platforms 'is illegal and strictly prohibited': P49.
units.anchor: uploading any course content to any online portal

units.why: Gives a stated consequence ('Level 3 or Level 4') for uploading course content: P37.
units.anchor: it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4

units.why: Every AI use 'must be properly and completely cited': P24.
units.anchor: the specific use of a G-AI tool must be properly and completely cited

units.why: Routine grammar-tool use needs only 'one citation for the entire document' in a set format (tool, date, version): P25. A lighter disclosure than P100, which exempts routine features.
units.anchor: use the following format with only one citation for the entire document
units.fit_note: Single citation for routine use, with prescribed fields.

units.why: Substantial uses need 'a separate citation for each use' in a format with tool, prompt, date and model: P25.
units.anchor: include a separate citation for each use

units.why: Says which prompts to include in citations ('first, second, and last prompt'): prompt details in citation (P25).
units.anchor: include the first, second, and last prompt with ellipses (...) in between

units.why: Faculty may require 'the entire transcript as an appendix', transcripts on request (P26).
units.anchor: include the entire transcript as an appendix

units.why: The example citation shows 'the lines obtained from this tool are indicated in the code', marking AI-derived code where used (P27).
units.anchor: the lines obtained from this tool are indicated in the code
units.fit_note: Stated through a citation example rather than an explicit rule.

units.why: Repeats in the suspected-misuse section that students must explain and demonstrate work: P30.
units.anchor: Students are always responsible for explaining, justifying, demonstrating their work

units.why: On suspicion faculty give the student a follow-up 'in-person oral or written' demonstration, an understanding check (P34); P64 (right to respond) fits less since the aim is verification.
units.anchor: provide an opportunity for the student to justify, explain, or demonstrate their work
units.fit_note: Also gives the student an opportunity to respond.

units.why: Failure to explain makes it 'an intentional academic integrity violation' at 'Level 3 or Level 4': penalty stated in advance (P37).
units.anchor: intentional academic integrity violation and will be reported as a Level 3 or Level 4

units.why: Faculty may compare writing style with an in-person sample, a kind of evidence in a misuse finding (P69).
units.anchor: compare your writing style obtained in an in-person writing assignment
units.fit_note: Names a specific evidence method (writing-style comparison).

units.why: Faculty may ask students to rewrite 'a paragraph or two, in person', an in-person check of authorship (P34).
units.anchor: may ask you to (re)write a paragraph or two,

units.why: Over-limit AI content 'will be reported as an academic integrity violation' at a level matched to the amount: reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: reported as an academic integrity violation, at a level appropriate to the amount

units.why: Missing or improper citation 'will be considered cheating/plagiarism': nondisclosure is the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Not citing or improperly citing the use of AI-generated content will be considered cheating/plagiarism

units.why: Treats fake citations and hallucinations as 'evidence of AI-generated content', an evidence standard (P69).
units.anchor: fake citations, references that do not actually exist

notes: Coded four included documents. The university-wide AI policy is an information-security policy; coursework is delegated to the Academic Integrity Policy and instructor syllabus statements. Two ECE uses (literature search, concept illustrations) were UNCOVERED.
